title: No time to lose
hookLine: Bahiya awakens on the spot, and dies soon after, gored by a cow

lines: LIFE IS UNCERTAIN, YOURS AND MINE.
cards: Someday I'll call my aunt. Someday I'll start sitting every morning. Someday I'll say sorry for that thing in college.
A someday list feels safe because it assumes there's time. Bahiya didn't assume it. When the Buddha told him twice that it wasn't the time, his answer was blunt: life is uncertain, yours and mine.
He'd come a long way to hear the teaching, and he wasn't willing to wait until after lunch. Today, how the story ends, and why it ends so fast.

teach.h: FREED, RIGHT THERE IN THE STREET.
teach.b: The text says that as he heard those few lines, in the seen only the seen, Bahiya's mind was freed, right there in the street. Then the Buddha went on with his alms round.

teach.h: A COW WITH A YOUNG CALF.
teach.b: And not long after, a cow with a young calf attacked Bahiya and killed him. That's the whole of it, in one sentence. On his way back, the Buddha saw the body.
He asked the monks to carry it on a litter, to cremate it, and to build a memorial mound for him.
When the monks asked what had become of Bahiya, the Buddha said: he was wise; he practiced in line with the teaching; he didn't trouble me with questions about it. He has reached final release.
Elsewhere in the canon, in a list of outstanding disciples, Bahiya is named foremost among those who understood quickly. Sit with the shape of the story.
A man traveled far, asked three times, heard a few lines, understood them, and died soon after.
If he had waited for the right time, there would have been no time. The early texts have a word for this kind of alertness: appamada, heedfulness, not letting things slide.
It doesn't mean panic. Bahiya wasn't frantic; he was clear. It means the good thing you can do today is today's.

how: Buddhist teachers sometimes tell Bahiya's story to illustrate appamada, heedfulness, and Theravada tradition, following the canon's list, remembers him as the disciple foremost in quick understanding.

o: heedfulness: not letting good things slide
rushing through life in a constant panic
a strict rule against wasting food

games.q: you're a monk with the Buddha. you find Bahiya's body by the road, killed by a cow. what does the Buddha ask you to do?
o: leave it; he wasn't ordained yet.
carry it, cremate it, and build a memorial mound.
games.why: he asks for full honor: a litter, cremation and a mound. then he tells the monks Bahiya has reached final release.

practice: Let your someday list come to mind, and find one small item on it: a message, a thank you, an apology, a few minutes of sitting. Picture yourself doing it today, where and when.
Then rest with the breath, calm, not hurried, knowing it's waiting for you.

wordCard.voice: Appamada, heedfulness. Bahiya asked to be taught at once, because life is uncertain; he understood at once, and died soon after.

orig.note: Pali appamada: heedfulness, diligence, not letting things slide.

carryVoice: Your line: today is today's. Being heedful doesn't mean being hurried. Day six hundred fourteen, done.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 1, Etadagga Vagga (Bahiya foremost in quick understanding)
